name: Docker
tagline: Runs apps as isolated Linux processes from layered images.

howItWorks.title: Namespaces: what a container sees
howItWorks.body:
A container is a process started with new namespaces.
pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc and user give a private view.
The kernel is shared; there is no hypervisor.
lsns lists them; nsenter -t PID -n enters one.

howItWorks.title: cgroups: what a container uses
howItWorks.body:
--memory is a hard cap on the whole cgroup, page cache included.
Over the cap, the kernel OOM-kills; docker inspect shows OOMKilled true, exit 137.
--cpus limits CPU time; --pids-limit caps process count.
cgroup v2 is the default on modern distributions.

howItWorks.title: Image layers
howItWorks.body:
An image is read-only layers addressed by content digest.
Each filesystem-changing instruction adds a layer.
Order instructions from stable to volatile to keep the cache.
overlay2 mounts layers as lowerdirs plus one writable upperdir.
Keep data in volumes, not the writable layer.

howItWorks.title: Bridge networks and veth
howItWorks.body:
Each container gets a veth pair; one end joins a Linux bridge.
The default docker0 bridge has no name resolution.
User-defined bridges add DNS at 127.0.0.11.
Published ports (-p) become iptables DNAT rules.
Outbound traffic is masqueraded to the host IP.

howItWorks.title: Compose profiles
howItWorks.body:
Compose declares services, networks and volumes in one file.
A profile starts a service only when requested.
Core services start by default; data and observability start on demand.
mem_limit on each service keeps a small host stable.

howItWorks.title: What sits in front
howItWorks.body:
Users and CI run the docker CLI, or Compose, against the dockerd Unix socket.
A reverse proxy on a user-defined network publishes the ports; the Edge sees only that proxy.
Registries such as Docker Hub or a private OCI registry supply images on pull.
Registry credentials live in ~/.docker/config.json.

howItWorks.title: What sits behind
howItWorks.body:
dockerd delegates to containerd, which calls runc to start the process.
The Linux kernel provides namespaces, cgroups, overlayfs and bridges (Infrastructure).
Volumes hold data; the json-file log driver holds output; cAdvisor can expose metrics.
The same OCI image later runs on Kubernetes through containerd or CRI-O.

howItWorks.title: Alternatives
howItWorks.body:
Podman: daemonless and rootless by default; choose it where no root daemon is wanted.
containerd with nerdctl: the runtime without the Docker daemon.
Buildah or Kaniko: image builds without a daemon, common inside CI.
LXC or a virtual machine: choose them when a full OS per workload is needed.

flow: docker run calls dockerd over the Unix socket.
dockerd pulls missing layers and verifies digests.
containerd mounts the layers as overlayfs with a writable layer.
runc creates namespaces and applies cgroup limits.
A veth pair joins the container to the bridge; an IP is assigned.
iptables adds DNAT rules for published ports.
The entrypoint starts as PID 1; the log driver captures output.
On exit or OOM, the restart policy decides what happens next.

deploy.summary: Prepare an Ubuntu Docker host, then inspect namespaces, cgroups, veth and layers.
prerequisites: Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 VM, 4 GB RAM, sudo user
A workstation with an SSH key pair
Static address and DNS record set by your network team

steps.title: SSH key login and sshd hardening
steps.code:
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub admin@<HOST_IP>
sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf <<'EOF'
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
MaxAuthTries 3
EOF
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh
steps.note: Keep your current session open and test a second login before logging out. Replace admin and HOST_IP.

steps.title: Install Docker Engine
steps.code:
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME) stable" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
steps.note: Log out and back in for the group change to apply. The docker group is root-equivalent.

steps.title: Daemon defaults
steps.code:
sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json <<'EOF'
{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" },
  "live-restore": true
}
EOF
sudo systemctl restart docker
steps.note: Without rotation, a chatty container fills the disk. live-restore keeps containers up during daemon restarts.

steps.title: Inspect namespaces and cgroups
steps.code:
docker run -d --name web --memory 128m nginx:1.27.3
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
sudo lsns -p $PID
sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip -br addr
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' web).scope/memory.max
steps.note: memory.max shows 134217728 on cgroup v2 with the systemd driver. The container has its own eth0.

steps.title: Bridge network and veth pairs
steps.code:
docker network create lab-net
docker run -d --name a --network lab-net nginx:1.27.3
docker run --rm --network lab-net busybox:1.36 nslookup a
ip -br link show type veth
bridge link show
sudo iptables -t nat -S POSTROUTING | grep MASQUERADE
steps.note: Each running container adds one veth on the host. User-defined networks resolve names through 127.0.0.11.

steps.title: Compose with profiles and memory limits
steps.code:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: lab
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.27.3
    ports: ["8080:80"]
    mem_limit: 128m
    restart: unless-stopped
  db:
    image: postgres:16.4
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: change-me
    mem_limit: 512m
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    profiles: [data]
volumes:
  pgdata:
EOF
docker compose up -d
docker compose --profile data up -d
docker compose ps
steps.note: The first command starts web only. The second adds db. Change the placeholder password.

steps.title: Trigger OOMKilled
steps.code:
docker run --name hog --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m python:3.12-slim \
  python -c "x = b'x' * (200*1024*1024)"
docker inspect -f 'OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' hog
docker rm hog
steps.note: Expect OOMKilled=true and exit=137. Raise the limit or fix the leak; never just remove the limit.

steps.title: Read the image layers
steps.code:
docker history nginx:1.27.3
docker image inspect -f '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}' nginx:1.27.3
docker system df
steps.note: Each row in history is a layer. Shared base layers are stored once.

verify: Namespaces exist: sudo lsns -p $(docker inspect -f "{{.State.Pid}}" web)
veth on bridge: bridge link show
DNAT rules present: sudo iptables -t nat -S DOCKER
pitfalls: Published ports bypass ufw rules; filter in the DOCKER-USER chain instead.
Unrotated json-file logs fill the disk.
Tight --memory limits cause OOMKilled with exit 137.
The default bridge has no DNS; use a user-defined network.
Never mount the Docker socket into an untrusted container.
Deleted files do not shrink earlier layers; use multi-stage builds.
Containers run as root by default; set a non-root USER.
keyPoints: Namespaces isolate what a container sees.
cgroups cap what it uses; exceeding the memory limit means OOMKilled.
Images are read-only layers; the container adds one writable layer.
Bridge networks connect containers over veth pairs and NAT.
quickDeploy: Install Docker Engine and set daemon log limits.
Inspect namespaces and cgroups of a running container.
Run a Compose stack with profiles and memory limits.
Trigger and read an OOMKilled exit 137.
osiNote: Bridges switch frames; iptables translates published ports.
production: Set memory and CPU limits on every container.
Run non-root with read-only root and dropped capabilities.
Pin image tags; scan images before they ship.
Alert on restarts, OOMKilled and docker system df growth.
